Mean body mass of newly hatched Pine warbler nestlings has been recorded at approximately 1.73 grams [Ww0 = approximately 1.73 grams]. Field observations indicate that when eggs are incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], hatching occurs after about 13 days [ab = about 13 days], a developmental period that is typical for small-bodied parulids. This brief incubation phase is followed by a rapid nestling growth period. Adult females ultimately attain a stable body mass of approximately 11.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 11.9 grams], reflecting the species’ relatively diminutive size compared to many other wood-warblers. The transition from the initial hatchling mass to the adult female mass represents a substantial proportional increase, underlining the metabolic demands of early development. During the nestling phase, chicks are entirely dependent on parental provisioning. This period of dependency concludes with fledging, which under the species’ typical active metabolic body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] occurs roughly 10 days after hatching [tx = roughly 10 days after hatching]. The brevity of this nestling stage is characteristic of many canopy-dwelling warblers and is linked to the high predation pressure experienced by open-cup nests.

Reproductive output in the Pine warbler is quantified by both clutch size and the frequency of nesting attempts. Females lay a single clutch of exactly 4 eggs per nesting event [N_R_i = 4 eggs per nesting event]. Given that this species typically completes only one successful brood per year [F_R_i = one successful brood per year], the annual reproductive rate is therefore 4 eggs per season. This pattern of producing a single small clutch annually is common among migratory warblers breeding in temperate North America. The first successful reproductive event for a female occurs 365 days after birth [tR = 365 days after birth], measured at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This timing means that birds hatched in one breeding season delay their own first breeding attempt until the subsequent year, a life-history schedule that allows for a full cycle of juvenile development, molt, and migration before engaging in the high energetic demands of territory establishment and nesting. The age at first reproduction thus corresponds to approximately one full year post-hatching.

The onset of reproductive capability, or puberty, in the Pine warbler is reached relatively early in life. Under the standard thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], male and female juveniles attain sexual maturity at approximately 30 days after hatching [tp = approximately 30 days after hatching]. This rapid gonadal development is somewhat earlier than the actual age at first breeding, indicating a delay between physiological maturity and the behavioral initiation of nesting. This decoupling is thought to reflect constraints imposed by the timing of spring migration and the need to establish a breeding territory. Although the birds are physically capable of reproduction by one month of age, the logistical requirements of the annual cycle—including the long-distance migration to wintering grounds and back—mean that first breeding is deferred to the following calendar year. The 30-day interval to puberty after hatching (30 days after hatching) [tp = 30 days after hatching] is nonetheless a key parameter for understanding the species’ potential population growth, as it sets a lower bound on generation time in the absence of migratory constraints at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

Basal metabolic rate measurements for the Pine warbler, obtained through closed-system respirometry, reveal a maximum oxygen consumption of 32 milliliters per hour [JOi = 32 milliliters per hour] when measured at a core body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This metabolic rate is consistent with the elevated mass-specific energetic demands typical of small passerines. The value reflects the high cost of endothermy in a bird with an average adult body mass of under 12 grams. Field studies have further documented the species’ maximum longevity in the wild. The longest-lived Pine warbler individuals, identified through banding returns, have been recorded surviving for approximately 6.8 years [am = approximately 6.8 years] under natural conditions, measured at the species’ characteristic active body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This lifespan is moderate for a New World warbler, balancing the high mortality rates of small-bodied migratory birds against the potential for multiple breeding seasons. The combination of a relatively high BMR and a moderate lifespan underscores the fast-paced life history strategy of this species.

In a comparative context, the Pine warbler’s life-history traits align closely with those of other Setophaga species that breed in the pine-dominated forests of the southeastern United States. The brief 13-day incubation period at 36 °C (13 days) [ab = 13 days] and the 10-day nestling stage at 41.6 °C (10 days) [tx = 10 days] are at the lower end of the observed range for parulids, reflecting the selective pressures of a short breeding season at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The ultimate wet weight of adult females, averaging 11.9 grams [Wwi = 11.9 grams], places Setophaga pinus among the smaller members of its genus. This small body size is ecologically linked to a foraging strategy focused on gleaning arthropods from the needles and branches of conifers. The annual reproductive output of 4 eggs per year is a precise constraint on the species’ demographic potential. Understanding the full suite of these life-history parameters—from a hatchling mass of 1.73 grams [Ww0 = 1.73 grams] to a maximal lifespan approaching 7 years—is essential for modeling the population dynamics of this pine-forest specialist under changing climatic conditions.
